extracted.intended_audience: lovers of poetry, literary critics, and educated general readers interested in literary aesthetics and cultural criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Literary-critical criteria for judging the quality and significance of poetry (and related cultural aims), with examples drawn from Wordsworth and other poets; aimed at selecting, appreciating, and defending poetic works. Emphasises what makes poetry 'great' and how culture should value intellectual life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet should 'deal with life' (dealings with what life really consists of)
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest poets 'deal with life' — that is, they treat what life really consists of; dealing with life (in this sense) is the mark of the high and genuine poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold holds this as a central standard: Wordsworth's greatness lies in his dealing with life as a whole and more powerfully than many other celebrated poets. Use this as a criterion when comparing poets: how fully and truly does the poet treat the substance of life?

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry (not philosophy) is the primary reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is the reality; philosophy, as a formal 'scientific system of thought' in poetry, is (so far as it assumes that form) an illusion that can obscure poetic truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of over-valuing explicit philosophical systems within poems. Arnold warns Wordsworthians who praise their poet chiefly for his 'philosophy'; the poetic effect — feeling and representation — should be primary. Dismissal of 'formal philosophy' is advised when it interferes with poetic reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth must have solidity — avoid abstract elevated verbiage
rubrics_metrics.description: Lines that are 'a tissue of elevated but abstract verbiage' lack the characters of poetic truth; poetic utterance must possess 'real solidity' rather than merely rhetorical, abstract declamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically distinguish between rhetorically lofty sentences and authentic poetic insight. Examples: passages from the Excursion are criticized as elevated yet abstract and alien to poetry. Favor concrete, solid poetic expression over abstract sermonizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not universalize doubtful propositions as poetic truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas (e.g. that childhood always supplies high instincts which fade) that are doubtful as universal statements lack the solidity required for the best poetic truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a poet's generalizations are empirically and emotionally convincing as universal claims. Arnold objects to treating the 'intimations' of childhood as a universally valid philosophical base — poetic assertions should not rest on insecure universal premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of poetic power: joy in nature and simple primary affections
rubrics_metrics.description: A chief source of Wordsworth's power is his extraordinary feeling and rendering of the joy offered in nature and in simple primary affections and duties; this joy is accessible universally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the poem communicates a sharable, profound joy rooted in nature and basic human affections. Arnold highlights the importance of accessibility and universality ('joy in widest commonalty spread') as a merit in poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of profound truth of subject and truth of execution
rubrics_metrics.description: The best poems perfectly balance profound truth of subject with profound truth of execution; where this balance succeeds, the poet is unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a compositional and evaluative standard: subject matter of genuine depth must be matched by execution (form, diction, rendering). Arnold cites Michael, The Fountain, The Highland Reaper as poems where this balance is achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspiration is crucial but irregular — greatness may coexist with lack of stylistic assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet may be overwhelmingly inspired at times ('filled with a new and sacred energy') and weak at others; Wordsworth often lacks an assured poetic style and when he attempts an over-conscious style falls into ponderosity and pomposity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging poets, account for unevenness: extraordinary inspired passages can outweigh periods of weakness, but consistent stylistic control is also valuable. Do not demand uniform inevitability of craftsmanship from all poets; note where inspiration produces 'inevitable' lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius for poetic style heightens verse and gives incomparable charm
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine poetic style — the subtle turn and heightening effected by style — is a distinctive source of a poem's power (examples: Shakespeare, Milton).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value those poets who possess an assured style that elevates even prosaic matter. Arnold contrasts Wordsworth's intermittent attainment of style with poets who consistently possess it, noting the special effect style has on poetic worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plainness and fidelity of expression can be a deliberate poetic strength
rubrics_metrics.description: A plain, austere manner, relying on the weight and force of genuinely felt material (as in Burns), can be supremely effective; baldness in expression can be grand when matched to subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate simplicity with weakness. Judge whether plain expression is truthful and fitting to the subject; Arnold praises Wordsworth's and Burns's use of a plain manner when it faithfully renders feeling and reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select representative works that best show a poet's characteristic power
rubrics_metrics.description: In editing or recommending a poet, choose poems that most perfectly show his unique power; avoid indiscriminate praise of every work merely because the poet is great.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold's anthology aim: present pieces that will 'best serve him with the majority of lovers of poetry' and avoid promoting works (e.g., _The Sailor's Mother_) that are failures despite the poet's overall greatness. Use discriminating selection rather than blanket inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of partisan or clique-like advocacy — recommend in the spirit of disinterested lovers of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: To secure rightful recognition for a poet, advocacy should be disinterested and not a clique's boosterism; exaggerating the poet's merits for the wrong things (e.g., formal philosophy) does harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and advocates should aim for impartial appreciation and avoid overstating aspects that are not central to poetic excellence. Arnold criticizes 'Wordsworthians' who praise the poet for his philosophical system rather than his poetic reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture's motive: prefer love of perfection to mere curiosity or exclusive learning
rubrics_metrics.description: True culture is not a vanity-driven smattering of classical learning but a study of perfection motivated by both scientific passion (desire to see things as they are) and the moral/social passion to do good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing cultural aims (including literary pursuit), favor motives that combine intellectual curiosity with social and moral aims. Arnold distinguishes between frivolous curiosity and the laudable scientific passion allied to social purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture must seek to make reason and moral will prevail (active mission)
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture should not only seek to know truth but to make reason and the will of God prevail; the study of perfection includes an active moral and social component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate cultural activities (including literature) by both their intellectual merits and their capacity to inform and improve social action. Arnold warns against culture that only sees without aiming to effect improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge greatness by spiritual standards, not material machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: Material goods and institutions (wealth, coal, railroads, population, bodily health) are 'machinery' and not ends in themselves; greatness should be judged as a spiritual condition that excites love, interest, and admiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate industrial/material success with national or human greatness. Arnold urges using a spiritual standard of perfection to evaluate societies and cultural achievements rather than measuring by material indices alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture opposes Philistinism: refine taste and resist vulgarization
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture purges the mind from worship of machinery and vulgar notions of greatness, cultivates taste ('sweetness and light'), and fosters dissatisfaction with merely material or vulgar ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cultural outputs (literature, manners, habits) for whether they elevate tastes and counteract Philistine tendencies. Arnold recommends scrutinizing the habits, literature, and speech of those who idolize wealth as evidence of cultural worth or lack thereof.
